960.title: Vincent of Saragossa (22 January)
960.hook: a deacon-martyr of Spain who spoke for his bishop, honored by vine-growers
960.tomorrow: Francis de Sales, patron of writers (24 January)
960.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Vincent's day in January, and in some wine regions growers mark it with a Mass and a blessing of the vines.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sebastian, the soldier who survived the arrows and went back to face the emperor. Your line was arrows didn't stop him.

Two prisoners stand before a Roman governor in Spain. One is old, a bishop, Valerius of Saragossa. The other is young, his deacon, Vincent. The governor asks his questions, and the bishop, the story says, struggles to get the words out. So the deacon asks permission to answer for them both. He speaks clearly and without fear, and the governor's patience snaps. The bishop is sent into exile. The deacon is kept back for something worse.
screen: `A BISHOP AND HIS DEACON, ON TRIAL.` → `THE BISHOP STRUGGLES TO SPEAK.` → `THE DEACON ANSWERS FOR BOTH.`

segments.voice: Vincent's story comes to us in poems and sermons of the early Church. The Christian poet Prudentius wrote a long hymn to him, and Augustine of Hippo preached on his feast. Start with what he was: a deacon. Behind that word is the Greek diakonos, a servant, someone who waits on others. In the Acts of the Apostles, the apostles choose seven men to serve the community's tables so that widows aren't forgotten, and Catholics see there the root of the job. Deacons serve the poor, read the Gospel at Mass, preach, and assist the bishop. Vincent served his bishop in a very literal way: as his voice. After the trial, the story is grim. Vincent was tortured, stretched and burned, and thrown into a cell on broken pottery. There, Prudentius sings, the dark cell filled with light, the shards turned soft as flowers, and the jailer was converted. Vincent died of his wounds, a deacon-martyr of Spain. Then the vines. In wine country, vine-growers took Vincent as their patron. People give different reasons, some half a joke about his name. His day falls in the dead of winter, when the vines are bare and pruning begins, and in some villages growers still walk out to bless the vines in his name. Some readers hear his feast in John's Gospel. Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the vine: you the branches". In the same chapter, the branches that bear fruit are pruned so they bear more. Winter work, on Vincent's day.
screen: `DIAKONOS: ONE WHO SERVES.` · `HE SPOKE FOR HIS BISHOP.` · `A DARK CELL FILLS WITH LIGHT.` · `WINTER VINES, BLESSED IN HIS NAME.` · then, large: `I AM THE VINE: YOU THE BRANCHES.`

segments.voice: Find a living plant near you, a houseplant, herbs on a sill, a tree outside the window, or bring one to mind, and look closely at the stems, the new growth, the dead leaves. Pick one dead leaf off gently, the way a vine-grower prunes in winter. If you pray, make the sign of the cross over it and ask God's blessing; if not, give it water and a moment of attention.
Diakonos, Greek for a servant, the word behind deacon. Vincent of Saragossa was one: he spoke for his bishop at trial, died a martyr, and is honored by vine-growers in the middle of winter.
Your line: a deacon of spain. He served his bishop by speaking up. See you tomorrow.

961.title: Francis de Sales, patron of writers (24 January)
961.hook: when no one came to hear him, he slid pamphlets under doors
961.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Francis de Sales's memorial in January; writers and journalists honor him as their patron, and his Introduction to the Devout Life is still read by lay Catholics.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vincent of Saragossa, the deacon who answered for his bishop. Your line was a deacon of spain.

A young priest stands in a village square in the hills south of Lake Geneva, ready to preach. Nobody comes. The town has become Reformed, Calvinist, and a Catholic preacher is not someone they want to hear. Doors stay shut; some people won't even look at him in the street. He could leave, or shout louder. Instead he sits down at a table and writes short pages, clear and calm, one argument at a time. Then, the story goes, he walks through town at night and slides them under the doors.
screen: `A PREACHER, AND NOBODY COMES.` → `HE SITS DOWN AND WRITES.` → `PAGES UNDER THE DOORS.`

segments.voice: Francis de Sales was a nobleman's son from Savoy who chose the priesthood over the career his father had planned. His bishop sent him to the Chablais, the region around those shut doors, to win people back to the Catholic Church. Catholics and Reformed Christians remember that time from two sides, and both remember a struggle. What Catholics remember about Francis is how he went about it: gently. His leaflets, later gathered into a book, read like letters, not attacks. Over the years, people in that region did come back to the Catholic Church, and the Church credits his patience. Later he became bishop of Geneva, though he lived across the border in Annecy, and he kept writing. His Introduction to the Devout Life was written for ordinary people, not monks. A holy life, he said, looks different for a soldier, a shopkeeper, a married woman, a bishop; devotion should fit the life you actually have, the way a bee takes honey from a flower and leaves it whole. With his friend Jane Frances de Chantal he also founded a community of sisters, the Visitation. The Church calls him a patron of writers. A Gospel line that fits him is Jesus in Matthew. In the Douay-Rheims: "learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart". Meek, in his hands, was not weak. It was the patience to write one more page and slip it under one more door.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose door is a little shut to you right now, someone you've drifted from or disagreed with, and write them a few plain, kind sentences in your head: clear, unhurried, no argument, no pressure to reply. If you pray, ask Francis de Sales to pray for the person who'd read it; if you don't, just hold their face in mind.
Francis. The bishop and writer Francis de Sales, who reached shut doors with gentle pages, and wrote that holiness should fit the life you actually have. A patron of writers.
Your line: slipped under the door. One calm page at a time. Day nine hundred sixty-one.

962.title: Timothy and Titus (26 January)
962.hook: Paul's young companions, whom he trusted with churches
962.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saints Timothy and Titus together, the day after the feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul, and the readings at Mass come from Paul's letters to them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis de Sales, who wrote calm pages for people who wouldn't hear him. Your line was slipped under the door.

Near the end of a letter, a prisoner adds a few errands. Hurry and come to me. Bring Mark with you. And the cloak I left at Troas, bring that too, and the books, especially the parchments. The letter is Second Timothy, and the prisoner is Paul: an apostle in chains, wanting his coat, his books, and his friend. The day after the feast of Paul's conversion, the Church keeps the feast of two people he trusted with whole churches. Timothy and Titus.
screen: `A PRISONER'S ERRANDS.` → `BRING THE CLOAK AND THE BOOKS.` → `AND COME YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Start with Timothy. Acts says Paul met him in Lystra: a young disciple whose mother was a Jewish believer and whose father was Greek. Paul took him along on the road. In the second letter, Paul remembers the faith that lived first in Timothy's grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice, and now in him. Timothy's faith came across a kitchen table, from two women, before it ever met an apostle. Paul sent him to the churches when he couldn't go himself, and later left him to care for the church at Ephesus. He knew people might not take a young man seriously, so he wrote, in the Douay-Rheims: "Let no man despise thy youth: but be thou an example of the faithful". Now Titus. Paul's letter to the Galatians says Titus was Greek. Paul brought him to Jerusalem, sent him to Corinth to help mend a broken relationship, then left him on Crete to set things in order and appoint priests, elders, in every city. Paul calls each of them his son in the faith. Not by blood; by years on the road. The Catholic Church keeps them on one day, as bishops, close behind Paul. Some readers hear a quiet point in their feast: a church grows through the younger people an apostle trusted, kept writing to, and kept encouraging. Paul even tells Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach. A mentor who notices your stomach means it.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone a step or two behind you, a new hire, a student, a niece starting out, someone who still gets talked over, and find one specific thing you've seen them do well: not a pep talk, one true detail. If you pray, pray for them by name, the way Paul did for Timothy; if you don't, simply hold their name and the good thing you noticed.
Timothy, with Titus. Paul's young companions and fellow workers, whom he trusted with churches in Ephesus and Crete, and called his sons in the faith.
Your line: paul's sons. Faith passed hand to hand, older to younger. That's day nine hundred sixty-two.

963.title: Angela Merici (27 January)
963.hook: she founded the Ursulines, women who stayed in their own homes and taught girls
963.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Angela Merici's memorial in January, and Ursuline sisters and schools around the world celebrate her as their founder.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Timothy and Titus, the younger men Paul trusted with churches. Your line was paul's sons.

In an Italian city, a group of young women want to give their whole lives to God. In their world, that usually meant one of two doors: marriage, or a convent behind a wall. A convent often meant a dowry, and some of them had nothing to bring; others had parents who needed them at home. An older woman named Angela, with no money and no title, opened a third door. Stay where you are. Live in your own homes. Belong to God anyway. And teach the girls of this city.
screen: `TWO DOORS: MARRIAGE OR A CONVENT.` → `SOME CAN'T TAKE EITHER.` → `ANGELA OPENS A THIRD.`

segments.voice: Angela grew up near Lake Garda in northern Italy and lost her parents young. She lived simply, as a laywoman connected to the Franciscans, and later settled in Brescia, where people came to her for advice. Tradition says that as a young woman she saw a ladder reaching up to heaven, with young women climbing it, and understood she would one day gather a community. In Brescia, she did: the Company of Saint Ursula, named for a legendary martyr who led a band of young women. The members took no vows in a cloister and at first wore no habit. They stayed with their families, met together, prayed, and taught girls the faith: holiness without the wall, carried into ordinary homes. Angela left her companions a Rule, some Counsels and a Testament, and what stands out is how much room she left. If times and needs changed, she told the leaders after her, they should make new rules or change things, carefully and with good advice. And things did change. After her death the Ursulines became religious sisters running schools, often within convents, and Ursuline schools spread. But it began with a woman and a handful of companions who refused to believe a girl's education could wait. Luke tells of Mary, Martha's sister, sitting at Jesus's feet to listen, a woman taking her place as a learner, and Jesus defending it. In the Douay-Rheims: "Mary hath chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her." Some readers hear Angela's whole work in that line.

964.title: Blaise (3 February)
964.hook: a bishop who, in his story, saved a boy choking on a fishbone; throats are blessed with crossed candles
964.howItsDone: On Saint Blaise's feast, Catholic parishes often offer the blessing of throats, with a priest or deacon holding two crossed candles at each person's throat while saying the blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Angela Merici, who opened a third door for women and set them teaching. Your line was teach the girls.

Early February, a weekday Mass, and at the end a line forms at the front. One by one, people step up, and the priest holds two long candles, crossed in an X and tied with a ribbon, gently against each throat. A short blessing, and they step aside. Kids giggle at the candles under their chins. Older people close their eyes. Someone with a cold coughs and gets blessed anyway. It's a gentle, slightly strange custom, and it belongs to a bishop called Blaise.
screen: `A LINE AT THE FRONT OF CHURCH.` → `TWO CANDLES, CROSSED.` → `AGAINST EACH THROAT.`

segments.voice: Blaise was a bishop of Sebaste, in Armenia, in the early centuries, and he died a martyr. That much the Church remembers. The rest comes from later stories, and the Church tells them as stories. In the first, Blaise is being led away under arrest when a mother pushes through the crowd with her son. The boy has a fishbone stuck in his throat and can't breathe. Blaise blesses him and prays, and the bone comes loose. The boy lives. In the second, a poor woman's only pig has been carried off by a wolf, and at Blaise's word the wolf gives it back. Later, when Blaise is in prison, she comes to see him, bringing food and candles to light his cell. A throat, and candles: put them together and you get the custom. On his feast, a priest or deacon holds two crossed candles at each person's throat and asks God, through the prayers of Saint Blaise, bishop and martyr, to free them from illness of the throat and from every other illness. The candles are not magic; in Catholic teaching a blessing is a prayer, not a charm. It puts a whole body, the part that swallows and speaks and sings, into God's hands for a moment. The Church prays a line from the Psalms at the start of each day in the Liturgy of the Hours. In the Douay-Rheims: "O Lord, thou wilt open my lips: and my mouth shall declare thy praise." A throat, opened, for praise.
screen: `A BISHOP AND MARTYR OF SEBASTE.` · `A BOY WITH A FISHBONE.` · `A WOMAN BRINGS CANDLES TO HIS CELL.` · `A BLESSING IS A PRAYER, NOT A CHARM.` · then, large: `O LORD, THOU WILT OPEN MY LIPS.`

965.title: Agatha (5 February)
965.hook: a Sicilian martyr, named at Mass, patron of Catania and of breast cancer patients
965.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Agatha's memorial in February; in Catania her feast is a great city festival with processions of her relics, and some hospitals and cancer support groups take her as patron.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Blaise, the bishop of the fishbone and the crossed candles. Your line was the blessing of throats.

At Mass, when the priest prays the Roman Canon, Eucharistic Prayer One, there's a moment near the end when he reads a little roll call of martyrs. Among them is a run of women's names: Felicity, Perpetua, Agatha, Lucy, Agnes, Cecilia, Anastasia. It goes by fast. But every time that prayer is said, a young woman from Sicily is named at the altar, alongside the apostles. The third name on that list: Agatha.
screen: `A ROLL CALL INSIDE THE MASS.` → `SEVEN WOMEN'S NAMES.` → `THE THIRD IS AGATHA.`

segments.voice: Agatha was a martyr of Catania, in Sicily, in the age of Roman persecution. That the Church honored her is clear: her name is in the Canon itself. The details come from a later account of her martyrdom, which the Church hands on as her story. In it, Agatha is a young Christian woman who has given her life to God. A powerful Roman official wants her, and when she refuses him, he turns her faith into a charge against her. She's sent away to be broken down, and isn't. At her trial she answers calmly. Then she's tortured, and the account is unflinching: her breasts are cut off. That night in prison, the story says, the apostle Peter comes to her in a vision and heals her wounds. She dies soon after, still refusing. It's a hard story. Tradition has made Agatha, who suffered in her body, a patron of women with breast cancer, and of nurses. Her city keeps her too. In Catania, people carry her relics through the streets on her feast, and tradition says that when the volcano Etna threatened the city, her veil was carried out to meet the lava. Paul, in his second letter to the Corinthians, hears Christ speak to him in his own weakness. In the Douay-Rheims: "My grace is sufficient for thee". Some readers hear Agatha's story in that line: a body hurt beyond fairness, and a grace that held.

966.title: Apollonia (9 February)
966.hook: an older woman martyred in Alexandria, remembered in a bishop's letter; patron of dentists
966.howItsDone: Catholics remember Saint Apollonia in February; she appears in art holding pliers with a tooth, and dentists and people with toothache ask her prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Agatha, the martyr of Sicily named at Mass. Your line was agatha of sicily.

A bishop in Alexandria writes to a fellow bishop about what he has just lived through: riots in his city, Christians dragged from their homes, beaten, killed in the streets. In the middle of his list he stops on one name, an older woman, and tells what the mob did to her. Later, painters would show her standing calmly with a pair of pliers, and in the pliers, a tooth. It looks almost comic until you know why. That letter is how we know Apollonia.
screen: `A BISHOP'S LETTER FROM ALEXANDRIA.` → `ONE NAME IN THE LIST.` → `A WOMAN HOLDING PLIERS AND A TOOTH.`

segments.voice: The bishop was Dionysius of Alexandria, and the historian Eusebius copied part of his letter into his Church History. Here's what Dionysius says, in plain words. A mob turned on the city's Christians. They seized Apollonia, whom he calls a marvelous older woman, a virgin. They beat her and broke out her teeth. Then they built a fire outside the city and told her to say their blasphemies or be burned alive. She asked for a moment. They let her go. And she stepped into the fire herself. That's the whole account, a few lines in a letter. Later writers asked hard questions about that last step, and the Church has still honored her as a martyr who would not deny Christ. The teeth explain the pliers, and the pliers explain the dentists: in time, people with toothache asked her prayers, and dentists took her as a patron. A strange road from a riot to a dental office, but a real one. A mob cornered an older woman, and she did not give way. Psalm seventy has an old person's prayer, in the Douay-Rheims: "Cast me not off in the time of old age: when my strength shall fail, do not thou forsake me." Look back at this week: Vincent speaking for his bishop. Francis de Sales sliding pages under doors. Timothy and Titus, trusted young. Angela teaching the girls. Blaise and the candles. Agatha of Sicily. And Apollonia, old, cornered, and faithful.

segments.voice: Run your tongue along your teeth: they chew, help you speak, let you smile. Bring to mind whoever has cared for them, a dentist, a hygienist, a parent who made you brush, and then an older person you know, and their strength. If you pray, ask Saint Apollonia to pray for them and for anyone in pain tonight; if you don't, hold them with thanks.
